title: Charles de Vilmorin Talks Career Pivot and New Collaboration With Shirtmaker Bourrienne
text:
Designer Charles de Vilmorin returns with a collaboration with French shirtmaker Bourrienne, stage costumes, and plans to revive his own label.
burst onto the sceneaward. In 2024, he launched a ready-to-wear line and dressed more than 150 participants for the opening ceremony of the 2024 Paris Summer Olympics.
Now the French designer is back with a new fashion collaboration and a career pivot. In his first interview since putting his eponymous brand on hiatus, Vilmorin revealed he’s been working on a slew of projects as a stage costume designer and animator, as well as a capsule line with French shirtmaker Bourrienne Paris X.“I never really took the time to step back and process it all.
It all became too much, and I went through a couple of tough years. Fortunately, I’ve found solace in costume design so right now, I’m working on a lot of stage productions,” he told WWD. After designing the holiday decorations for French department store Galeries Lafayette in 2023, he was approached to create the costumes for the musical “Une Seconde Avant Noël,” or “One Second Before Christmas” in English, set to premiere at the Folies Bergère theater next December.
Vilmorin is also working on costumes for Theater Basel’s upcoming production of the opera “Lucia di Lammermoor,” with sets by Pierre Yovanovitch, and for the ballet “Coppélia” at the Teatr Wielki in the Polish town of Lodz.
“Live performance is truly what I love most. It’s always been my dream. When I was little, I wanted to be a director, so this didn’t just come out of nowhere,” he said.
“I’m not saying I don’t want to return to fashion. I’d love to come back and do another runway show in a year’s time,” he added.
“But it was important to find inspiration elsewhere. ”Vilmorin is working to get his label up and running again after parting ways with his former business associates, amid a shrinking wholesale sector, soft consumer spending, trade volatility and rising costs that have “I made quite a few management errors because I was handling everything on my own. These are complex things to get back on track.
Right now, the priority is to establish a stable, healthy structure again,” he said, adding that he’s kept the rights to his name. The designer is also developing an animation series based on his signature swirly, fantastical drawings.
“It will tell the story of my own psychological journey over the past few years through fictional characters. It’s going to be very dreamlike,” he teased. , who also worked on the project. Together with the label’s creative director Cécile Faucheur, he’s developed four ready-to-wear and three haute couture designs to be presented during an intimate event on Saturday at the Hôtel de Bourrienne, whose 18th-century decor inspired the collection.
“It’s a private residence steeped in history, as it was once the home of Fortunée Hamelin — a woman who, during the Directoire era, was a true trailblazer and a major figure in Parisian high-society nightlife, constantly hosting soirées and balls there. You can really feel it; there’s a real atmosphere of celebration and joy,” he said.
Hamelin was one of the Merveilleuses, female members of a fashionable aristocratic subculture with distinct dress codes that flourished in the immediate aftermath of the French Revolution as a rebellion against the Reign of Terror. Fond of wearing gauzy white dresses and tunics modeled after the ancient Greeks and Romans, they inspired all-white looks including the Fortunée shirt, which comes with a detachable ruffled collar.
Nikita Vlassenko, Cécile Faucheur, Charles de Vilmorin and Carine Beigbeder during a fitting at the Hôtel de Bourrienne. The Thérésa, named after socialite Thérésa Tallien, is a laced bib top embroidered with two stylized swans, borrowed from the hand-painted interiors that were painstakingly restored after French entrepreneur Charles Beigbeder acquired the property.
His wife Carine Beigbeder, cofounder and chief executive officer of Bourrienne, said the collaboration with Vilmorin is part of the brand’s efforts to raise its visibility as the company enters its next phase of growth, with plans to open a second store in Paris this year. With only a handful of wholesale partners, including Le Bon Marché in Paris, Lane Crawford in Hong Kong and Swiss department store Bongénie, it has developed a solid direct-to-consumer business, registering strong online sales in the United States and Japan, in particular.
Bourrienne’s sales rose by more than 50 percent in the first six months of the year, and posted a similar jump in 2025 as a whole, she reported.
“We need to be careful not to move too fast, in order to remain consistent. But at the same time, we need to build brand awareness to grow sales so we can invest in new projects,” she said. Bourrienne was launched in 2018 as a men’s line, adding women’s shirts the following year. Its first collaboration was with Olivier Theyskens, and women now account for 55 percent of sales, versus 45 percent for men, Beigbeder said.
“We’re very selective with our collaborations,” she noted. “We choose only projects that make sense and align with our vision. ” She praised Vilmorin for being attuned to the history of the brand’s headquarters, and bringing a welcome touch of drama to the line.
“Bourrienne was a little more classic. Charles has a more theatrical vision of fashion, and I feel like the combination of the two makes for something really special,” said the executive. Vilmorin noted the shirt is one of his favorite wardrobe staples.
“I’ve always loved making and wearing them,” he said. While the ready-to-wear items retail for between 380 euros for a bib top and 1,100 euros for a shirtdress, he will also take custom orders for the more elaborate pieces, which feature details like porcelain buttons.
“I hadn’t sewn for two years, but now I’m back to making dresses at home — something I’d missed terribly. Poplin is such a joy to work with; I’m really having a blast,” he said. WWD and Women's Wear Daily are part of Penske Media Corporation. © 2026 Fairchild Publishing, LLC. All Rights Reserved.
